item.title: Concrete Floods Walls and an Elevated East River Park Now Protect a Swath of Lower Manhattan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant environmental project with technical detail and useful vocabulary.

The most critical parts of the East Side Coastal Resiliency Project’s flood protection system may be the ones New Yorkers will never see.

In the new John V. Lindsay East River Park in lower Manhattan, engineers have been working on an ambitious challenge: protecting the park and surrounding neighborhoods from coastal flooding.

Beneath a 2-foot-thick concrete wall designed to hold back coastal flooding, steel structures extend deep underground, anchoring the barrier and helping prevent water from finding a way underneath it.

Depending on the location, engineers supported the wall with steel sheets driven into the ground or large underground pipes. The latter were used in areas where existing utility lines prevented the installation of a continuous barrier, explained Eric Ilijevich, a director at the city’s Department of Design and Construction.

But keeping floodwater from flowing over the wall is only part of the challenge. Water can also seep through the soil beneath it. To prevent this, engineers installed underground barriers using a technique called jet grouting, which involves injecting cement-based material into the ground to seal gaps.

The greatest danger is not seepage during a single storm, but the cumulative damage caused by repeated flooding. Over time, water moving through the soil could erode the ground supporting the wall, potentially undermining the entire structure.

The system, nearing completion, is designed to protect against flooding up to 16.5 feet above sea level, but engineers built in an additional two feet of protection, bringing it to 18.5 feet in case the team “was wrong in their projection,” said Joseph G. Lione, associate commissioner for coastal resiliency at the Department of Design and Construction of New York City.

The East Side Coastal Resiliency Project, which extends from East 25th Street along the East River to Montgomery Street, between the Williamsburg and Manhattan Bridges, was developed in response to the devastation caused by Hurricane Sandy in 2012, when a storm surge flooded large parts of Lower Manhattan, including the neighborhoods surrounding East River Park. The disaster exposed the vulnerability of the city’s waterfront communities to coastal flooding, a threat expected to grow as sea level rises.

The $1.45 billion project aims to protect approximately 110,000 New Yorkers on Manhattan’s East Side from coastal flooding. It involves raising sections of East River Park by 8 to 10 feet and installing a system of floodwalls, berms and movable floodgates along the waterfront on either side of the elevated park.

Construction began in 2020 and is expected to be completed in 2027. Right now, only the northern section of the park is still under construction. “We’ve successfully completed over $1 billion” in construction, said Lione.

More than half of the park has now reopened to the public. Lione said the city was required to keep at least 41 percent of the park open throughout construction.

“They did a good job at keeping the park open,” said Wendy Brawer, a member of the Community Advisory Group and director of Green Map System, a sustainability nonprofit.

Raising the park has also improved accessibility by bringing it roughly to street level, as the city built bridges for better pedestrian access from the Lower East Side. “If the water rises, it will go on the steps; the park is now too high to be flooded,” said Lione.

The rebuilt park will also feature a continuous bike lane, “which the community really wants,” said Lione.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

The project also relies on an extensive flood-protection system, much of it hidden beneath the rebuilt park.

The East Side Coastal Resiliency Project first took shape twelve years ago, in 2014.

But in 2018, the city announced a major redesign that would require raising and rebuilding much of East River Park. The decision sparked fierce opposition from residents and environmental activists, who opposed the destruction of mature trees and the prolonged loss of access to one of the neighborhood’s few green spaces during construction. “It was difficult to start with activists a few years ago,” Lione remembers.

Despite protests and legal challenges, construction began near East 25th Street, at the northern end of the project, before reaching East River Park in December 2021. “Now, we have very little pushback,” said Lione. “People understood what it was for.”

But opposition to the project has not disappeared.

“We still exist,” said Pat Arnow, co-founder of the East River Park Action, one of the major community advocacy groups that has opposed the city’s redesign of the park since 2018.

Arnow is no longer calling for a different flood-protection plan, although she maintains that “they could have provided the same amount of flood protection without destroying the entire park.”

For East River Park Action, the main concern is now the lack of shade in the rebuilt park following the removal of mature trees. The newly planted trees are still small, offering little protection from the sun. A few umbrellas provide some shade, but large stretches of the park remain exposed, with concrete surfaces absorbing heat.

“Those little umbrellas don’t do too much,” Arnow said. Brawer estimates that it will take 40 years for the new trees to provide comparable benefits.

New York City plans to plant 2,000 trees, said Lione. So far, the construction team planted about 600.

Lione said many of the removed trees were in poor condition because of exposure to saltwater from the East River. This is something Arnow believes is not true: “We have proof that they were growing,” she said.…

item.title: Tequila’s hangover: How the drink’s success drove deforestation in Mexico
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the environmental impact of a popular product with clear context and useful vocabulary.

- Between 2017 and 2022, increased tequila production in Mexico drove greater demand for its raw material, blue agave, but also caused social and environmental damages.

- The tequila regulatory body and state authorities have failed to halt the expansion of agave into forest areas.

- Jalisco lost around 23,368 hectares (about 57,740 acres) of forest annually between 2019 and 2021, a period that coincided with the expansion of blue agave fields.

- Between 2017 and 2025, the area planted with tequila agave nationwide increased by 218%, reaching 276,043 hectares (about 682,110 acres).

For decades, Manuel García Castro has grown corn, squash and beans to feed his family and livestock. In 2019, he followed in the footsteps of prosperous local farmers and dedicated a portion of his land in the highlands of Jalisco, western Mexico, to planting blue agave, used to make tequila.

A friend persuaded him to plant 15,000 shoots on 3 hectares (7.41 acres) of his land and in other areas where his cattle grazed. García Castro would provide the labor; his friend, the capital. “We have to give it a shot to see if there’s some way to make money from something else,” was their thinking, he told Mongabay. Back then, raising livestock didn’t bring in much money and expenses were high.

They invested 500,000 Mexican pesos (around $25,300) in plants, pesticides and fertilizers, not including payment for García Castro’s own labor and that of the farm worker who helped him. Four years later, in 2023, hopes of selling the blue agave began to fade. Sale prices per kilogram plunged by as much as 92% compared with those between 2017 and 2019. The business was no longer profitable in the short term. Manuel García and his partner abandoned the fields two years ago.

The tequila boom

Tequila has a protected designation of origin in the states of Guanajuato, Nayarit, Tamaulipas, Michoacán and Jalisco. The drink is considered a national brand and a symbol of Mexican identity.

Over the past decade, the tequila industry has boosted its exports and developed premium and niche brands.

Between 2016 and 2025, the Tequila Regulatory Council (CRT) recorded an increase in production from 273.3 million liters (72.2 million gallons) to 583.5 million l (154 million gal). Production peaked at 651.4 million liters in 2022.

In 2020, Mexico exported 286.7 million l (75.7 million gal) of tequila, and 418.9 million l (110.6 million gal) two years later.

Between 2017 and 2018, the sale price of blue agave remained between 26 and 30 pesos per kilogram (just under $2), peaking in 2021 at 32 pesos per kilogram, according to industry website agaves.pro.

Those economic conditions attracted new producers, including Manuel García, who replaced corn on his plots with blue agave.

Agave replacing forests

In 2019, when blue agave prices boomed, Maximiano Bautista Andalón, a geospatial specialist and academic at the Western Institute of Technology and Higher Education (Iteso) in Mexico, began using satellite imagery to document the expansion of agave farms in Jalisco.

That year, he counted roughly 100,000 hectares (about 247,100 acres) planted with agave only in Jalisco. Six years later, the area had reached 200,000 hectares (494,210 acres). The researcher found that this expansion affected natural ecosystems and created monocultures, as many farmers stopped growing food while others took over forest and rainforest areas.

“Agave is a complex issue, especially because of how it was distributed: in areas with pine forest, oak forest, or right next to mid or high-altitude areas where other crops used to grow,” Bautista Andalón said. “It is a highly industrial model in which almost no other little plant survived among the agave fields.”

In 2023, a report by the University of Guadalajara and a coalition of 43 states and provinces from 11 countries, including Mexico, highlighted the expansion of agave production for tequila and mezcal as one of the drivers of forest loss.

“The increase in demand and prices for these distilled beverages, especially tequila, has triggered a cyclical expansion of agave cultivation into these ecosystems,” the report warns. Between 2019 and 2021, a period coinciding with the tequila boom, Jalisco recorded its highest deforestation levels losing 23,368 hectares (about 57,740 acres) annually.

Neither the National Forestry Commission (Conafor) nor the Jalisco Department of Environment and Territorial Development responded to Mongabay’s interview requests for this article.

The agave landscape around the town of Tequila, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in western central Mexico, has spread indiscriminately across the state.

By analyzing satellite imagery, researcher Bautista Andalón found that some of the newest agave plantations were preceded by fires, land clearing or tree cutting, or were established near water sources important to local communities.

Southern Jalisco is also experiencing the impacts of agave expansion. University of Guadalajara researcher Oscar Raúl Mancilla is part of a scientific group that has studied land-use change in the region for 20 years and found that blue agave cultivation increased by 60% in the Autlán region, in southwestern Jalisco, between 2015 and 2026.

“Thousands of hectares have shifted from tropical dry forest, livestock farming or other types of crops to agave cultivation,” Mancilla told Mongabay.

Crossing the boundary

The area planted with tequila agave nationwide increased 218% between 2017 and 2025, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development

In 2021, the Tequila Regulatory Council (CRT) and the Jalisco government implemented the Environmentally Responsible Agave (ARA) certification to guarantee deforestation-free brands that comply with international sustainability standards.…

item.title: Relearning how to live with wolves in Europe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engages with a conservation issue in Europe with a nuanced perspective and useful vocabulary.

Across much of Europe, gray wolves were hunted to near extinction by the mid-20th century. In the past couple of decades, though, strict protections have helped the population rebound in some countries.

The return of the gray wolf (Canis lupus) has posed a conundrum. Conservation groups view it as a conservation success. However, wolves sometimes kill livestock, which brings them into conflict with some farmers. In response, the European Union recently weakened the wolf protections, making it easier to hunt the animals.

In a conversation with Mongabay’s Mike DiGirolamo, social scientist Emu-Felicitas Ostermann-Miyashita, from the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, argues the situation shouldn’t be seen as wolves versus livestock, but rather “livestock with wolves.”

“Looking back to the point when wolves were abundant in the landscape, it has always been livestock with wolves because people had no other choice,” Ostermann-Miyashita says in the Newscast episode. “And that’s why in the countries where there has been persistent wolf populations without them being exterminated … these protection measures are intact, like fencing or putting the sheep into enclosures during the evening to prevent livestock predation.”

By contrast, landscapes where wolves have been extinct for decades or centuries have become more populated with humans who have become habituated to living without wolves, Ostermann-Miyashita says. So the knowledge of how to protect livestock from large carnivores has also been lost, she adds.

Ostermann-Miyashita has studied the conflict between humans and wolves in Germany, where the canids were once exterminated and have since returned. In early 2025, she published suggestions for wolf-livestock coexistence.

One of these suggestions is for European countries to collaboratively assess their approaches to managing interactions with wolves. Ostermann-Miyashita says there are four broad ways to manage large carnivores across Europe: protect livestock using methods like fencing; provide compensation or financial measures for livestock losses; pay people for letting carnivores persist on their land; and lethal control.

Ostermann-Miyashita says it’s important that countries like Germany, which now have decades of experience with the return of wolves, share their experience with countries that are newer to wolf reintroduction, like the Netherlands or Belgium. This way, everybody doesn’t have “to go through the same process to adapt to the species,” Ostermann-Miyashita adds.

The effectiveness of each management method is highly context-dependent, Ostermann-Miyashita says, adding that more research is needed.

There are some studies to suggest that killing wolves, for example, may reduce damage temporarily by getting rid of a pack or an individual, but another wolf pack can fill its gap and the damage can restart, Ostermann-Miyashita says. “So at the moment, I would say there’s not enough evidence to say whether lethal control can be effective or not.”

item.title: International marine biodiversity conference emphasizes the unsung and the unknown
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Focuses on an international conference with implications for marine biodiversity, offering a broad view.

- More than 800 people gathered Nov. 17-20 in Bruges, Belgium, for the 7th World Conference on Marine Biodiversity.

- The conference covered a wide range of science and conservation topics, including the impacts of deep-sea mining; it featured a screening of a documentary that follows scientists on a deep-sea mission to an area in the Pacific Ocean targeted for deep-sea mining.

- The conference took place just after the midway point of the U.N. Ocean Decade, which runs 2021-2030, and the organizers called it a chance to take stock of progress.

BRUGES, Belgium — More than 800 people gathered for the 7th World Conference on Marine Biodiversity, held Nov. 17-20, in Bruges, Belgium.

The conference took on topics as varied as deep-sea mining impacts, ocean-related art, citizen science, methods for working with large datasets, environmental DNA and taxonomy. Yet it also raised broader questions about how people value the ocean and whether current approaches serve the health of marine ecosystems. David Obura, founder of Kenyan marine research nonprofit CORDIO East Africa, gave the opening keynote, calling for a shift in thinking about how people use the sea.

“If we just use the same values that have historically driven current markets to maximise further benefits from oceans … we just drive oceans farther into decline,” Obura told Mongabay in an email recapping his talk. “We’ve seen this already. Instead we need to apply values that prioritise balance and sustainability across multiple co-benefits, and deliver long term security and prosperity over short term gain.”

Many participants emphasized the need to catalog the world’s marine biodiversity and draw attention to overlooked species or those not yet described.

“We want to see how many species are there because we want to know what we need to conserve,” Bert Hoeksema, a guest researcher at Naturalis Biodiversity Center, a museum in the Netherlands, told Mongabay. Hoeksema has studied corals for more than four decades and recently published a paper identifying key countries involved in the marine aquarium trade. “There are so many species that are not known.”

The conference took place just after the midway point of the U.N. Ocean Decade, which runs 2021-2030. The initiative, decided by the U.N. General Assembly in 2017, aims to promote ocean science and use it to guide policy to support ocean health.

“It’s an excellent moment to take stock,” Leen Vandepitte, a conference organizer and project manager of the Flanders Marine Institute’s (VLIZ) data center, told Mongabay. “Where are we? Where do we still need to go?”

Worming out

The conference has its roots in the European marine research community. The first edition took place in Valencia, Spain, in 2008, near the end of a five-year EU-funded research project on marine biodiversity. The 2026 conference happened to follow a marine conservation conference held Nov. 13-16 in Edinburgh.

For the seventh edition, scientists, conservationists, policymakers and industry members gathered in Bruges, in Belgium’s Dutch-speaking Flanders region. They addressed issues such as plastic pollution in the ocean, how climate and fisheries impacts interact, and mangrove restoration in Latin America and the Caribbean.

VLIZ, the conference’s organizer, hosts the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS), an inventory of the more than 250,000 marine species that are currently known to science. About 350 taxonomists help maintain WoRMS, adding some 2,000 newly described species each year, while estimates of the total number of marine species that exist range from 500,000 to 2 million, according to VLIZ.

Among the overlooked animals discussed at the conference were nematodes, small roundworms that live in the seafloor in astonishing numbers, which serve a key role as nutrient recyclers. Lara Macheriotou, a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University, spoke about how a deep-sea mining trial affected nematode diversity, drawing on samples collected before, during and after.

The Flanders-based company Global Sea Mineral Resources conducted the trial in 2021 in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean, a deep-sea abyssal plain located between Hawai‘i and Mexico. Ghent University, which is also in Flanders, is home to several researchers studying the potential impacts of deep-sea mining for polymetallic nodules, which are potato-sized lumps containing sought-after metals such as manganese. Many animals, like nematodes, live on them or in their crevices. Deep-sea mining hasn’t been done at a commercial scale.

Ann Vanreusel, an emeritus professor of marine biology at Ghent University who attended the conference, said the prospect of deep-sea mining was “concerning because you’re impacting a pristine untouched environment.” It also changed the nature of her work, which had been pure research aimed at building core knowledge of the sea and then became more oriented around mining-related questions.

“I could do 30 years of fundamental research with not any societal connection, and then all of a sudden you get deep-sea mining,” she told Mongabay.

Many sessions at the conference dealt with scientific methods such as environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis, which can detect the presence of species — many species, all at once — from traces of DNA they leave in the water. Such powerful molecular techniques can save scientists a lot of time and money. Yet several scientists stressed the continued importance of old-school taxonomic work that involves examining specimens to identify and describe them. Vanreusel said she was worried that this taxonomic expertise was being lost.

One session focused on the need for greater support and investment for taxonomic work in Africa.…

item.title: How Uttarakhand’s women farmers are reviving endangered Himalayan medicinal plants
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Describes a community-driven conservation effort with cultural and environmental significance.

- In Uttarakhand, India, high-altitude farmers are cultivating medicinal herbs that are in decline in the wild, helping these species revive.

- Women perform most of the labor in this enterprise, earning money to support their families and children’s education.

- Obstacles remain, however, as farmers often must obtain official certification requiring proof of land ownership — and only a small percentage of women own land in the region.

- “Because of this, we insist on issuing the certification in the female farmer’s name,” says Shivam Pandey of Udyogini, an NGO working toward women’s empowerment.

RAMNI, Uttarakhand, India — At state fairs across Uttarakhand, while most farmers set up stalls featuring local millet varieties, Guddi Devi and her fellow farmers showcase saplings of high-altitude medicinal plants.

“In the past, people used to bring kutki [Picrorhiza kurroa] and other herbs like sugandha bala [Valeriana jatamansi] from the bugyals [alpine meadows]. Since everyone was going there, digging and harvesting, everything was becoming extinct in the alpine meadows. It is a cumbersome task to even reach there, so you won’t easily find [these herbs] there anymore,” Guddi said.

Situated in the Indian Himalayan region, Uttarakhand’s medicinal plants, growing at 2,000 meters (6,500 feet) or more, are highly sought after. Traditionally, locals traveled up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) on foot to collect herbs like kutki — widely used to bring down fevers — when access to medical care was scarce. Globally, market demand for medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs) has grown substantially, with $4.2 billion in exports in 2023, and due to unsustainable harvesting practices and overexploitation, many species are at risk.

With growing concern, scientists say controlled agricultural cultivation can be a sustainable method to meet the pharmaceutical demands for these plants.

“Uttarakhand has diverse agro-climatic conditions, therefore, mountain villages located at about 2500 to 3000 m altitude are suitable locations for domestication or for cultivation of high altitude medicinal and aromatic plants,” known as MAPs, Chandra P. Kuniyal, a scientist at the Herbal Research and Development Institute (HRDI), said in an email.

Since men of the hills often leave their homes for better financial opportunities, it is the women living in villages at high altitudes — where these MAPs thrive in the cold — who have become the cornerstone of medicinal herb conservation efforts.

“The feminization of hill agriculture is there because mostly the men migrate outside for their job,” said K.S. Kanwal, scientist at G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment.

Conservation through cultivation

“The goal is to conserve these species outside their natural habitats,” Kanwal said.

India is home to 8,000 medicinal plant species, of which 140 have been prioritized for national cultivation support. Uttarakhand has listed 38 such species. Because rising commercial demand threatens wild populations, both in situ (in-nature) and ex situ (off-site cultivation) strategies are being deployed.

In situ conservation focuses on preserving species within their natural environment by restricting harvesting or creating protected areas, providing protection to the species as well as the critical habitat. Kuniyal notes that in remote mountain terrains, limited enforcement personnel and strong illicit trade networks make in situ protection insufficient on its own.

This gave way to ex situ conservation strategies, particularly the cultivation of MAPS. Scientists assess species based on market demand and threat levels defined by the IUCN and the Indian Red Data Book.

“After prioritizing target species at state and regional levels, comprehensive conservation plans are drawn up, raising plants in institute nurseries and establishing new propagation sites directly in farmers’ fields,” Kanwal said.

It is mostly women who are engaged in agriculture in the mountains. “Not only do they know how to cultivate but they are micro-observers too. If there is something, an issue, any disease, another thing, they immediately inform us,” Kanwal said.

While women are key agricultural workers here, men help in transporting the material to nearby collection or purchasing destinations and also marketing the herbs.

Ecosystem conservation

Once species are selected by government scientific bodies like HRDI and the GB Pant Institute, saplings are distributed to high-altitude farmers either directly or through partner NGOs like Udyogini, which works with thousands of farmers across six regions in Uttarakhand. The central goal of Udyogini is women’s empowerment. For women in extreme remote villages, agriculture is a source of autonomy.

“Udyogini provides us with 2,000 free saplings for a 1-naali plot,” 200 square meters or 2,160 square feet, Guddi explained. “We receive plants based on our land size, and the plots are officially registered. With experience, we now know exactly how many plants a field can accommodate and how to plant them properly.”

Because these herbs need cooler conditions, cultivation cannot take place in lower village plots. The women farmers hike half a kilometer (0.3 miles) uphill to tend fields that were previously wastelands. Beyond farm plots, project interventions have also reintroduced rare and threatened species back into six degraded high-altitude pasture lands called bugyals.

The project also addresses another major agricultural challenge: human-wildlife conflict. Traditional crops are frequently destroyed by wild boars and monkeys, but wild animals often leave medicinal herbs untouched, offering farmers a viable way to utilize abandoned land. (In a recent study, for example, it was shown that some MAPs, containing antifeedants or chemicals that are unpalatable to pests, were less attractive to elephants than rice crops.)…

item.title: US gains foothold in race for Africa’s critical minerals in Kenya’s Mrima Hill project
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Reports on a mining project with implications for Africa's critical minerals, though less detailed.

Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Mining and Blue Economy has announced that the mining ministry has issued a “notice of intention” to award the tender for the development of the Mrima Hill mining project to U.S.-based mining consortium Frontier Minerals. Mrima Hill is thought to be rich in critical minerals sought after by electronics, aerospace and energy industries,

“The choice of an American consortium reflects a commitment from the Kenyan government to develop their mining sector in a transparent manner that will bring market-leading innovation to Kenya, ensure local value addition, and create jobs and economic benefits [for the U.S. and Kenya],” said the U.S. State Department in a statement.

The U.S.’s interest in Kenya’s critical minerals is part of Washington’s effort to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the critical minerals market.

According to Kenya’s Ministry of Mining, Mrima Hill holds at least 5.8 million tons of material that may contain niobium pentoxide, which is used to make niobium, a critical element used in electronics, the aerospace industry and energy storage. Two-thirds of the world’s niobium reserves are currently held by Brazil; the remaining third are mostly held by China. The region is also potentially home to millions of metric tons of rare earth elements (REEs), which are key components in the manufacture of batteries, magnets, mobile phones and cars.

While in its statement, the U.S. State Department emphasized transparency in the mining sector, Kenyan civil society organizations raised concerns that the process has not fully included local communities. According to Kenya’s Ministry of Mining, a company must first obtain the consent of local communities before it can secure a mining license. However, in June 2026, the Centre for Litigation Trust (CLT) filed a petition with the High Court in Kwale County, southern Kenya, where the mining concession is located, alleging the agreement process in Mrima Hill “has been shrouded in secrecy and undertaken without public participation.”

CLT is seeking to suspend the agreement until local communities are fully involved in the negotiations.

Environmental impacts are another concern. Mrima Hill is located about 65 kilometers (40 miles) south of Mombasa, Kenya’s second-largest city and a major tourist destination on the Indian Ocean coast. Mrima Hill is also part of the Eastern African coastal forests ecoregion. It’s home to numerous bird species, including near-threatened Fischer’s turaco (Tauraco fischeri) and the vulnerable spotted ground thrush (Geokichla guttata).

According to the Kenya-based environmental organization Nature Kenya: “Exploration activities have already disturbed the habitat through excavation pits, vegetation clearance, and increased human activity in sensitive forest areas. Large-scale mining would accelerate forest degradation, habitat fragmentation, soil erosion, and water pollution, while also threatening the sacred Kaya sites of the local Digo community.”

Banner image: Niobium crystal bar, Niobium is used as an alloying agent in steels and in high-tech applications, such as electric car batteries. Image by Dnn87 via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0).

item.title: US bill to speed up clean energy projects could also fast-track fossil fuels
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Examines a complex policy issue with potential environmental implications, but less focused on concrete detail.

On Nov. 19, the U.S. Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects.

The 62-33 vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) included support from pro-environment Democratic senators like Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island.

The legislation would ease development for renewable energy and transmission lines, but environmental organizations warn it will also fast-track fossil fuels by undermining environmental regulations.

“A technology-neutral fast track in the hands of an administration openly hostile to clean energy is not a bargain. It is a one-way ratchet for fossil fuels,” Brad Campbell, CEO of the Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement.

Currently, new U.S. infrastructure projects must comply with bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). If BAAJA becomes law, those environmental hurdles will become easier to clear.

Fewer projects would require NEPA review, the time frame for environmental assessments would be shorter, and the window to sue over approved projects would shrink. Consultation on potential impacts to endangered species would also be shortened.

Proponents of the bill say those changes would ease renewable energy development and lower U.S. carbon emissions.

“BAAJA is a big step forward in our fight against climate change,” Whitehouse, who co-sponsored the bill, wrote on social media. “The bill lowers emissions by 1.5 gigatons through 2040.”

However, the weakened environmental review would also apply to fossil fuel projects and data centers. In an open letter, more than 120 scientists urged the House of Representatives to reject the bill.

On land, BAAJA could lower barriers for oil, gas and mining projects on public and tribal lands. Several Native American organizations have condemned the bill.

At sea, BAAJA would “roll back ocean and wildlife protections, opening the door to more offshore oil and gas drilling, more pollution, and greater threats to marine life,” U.S.-based NGO Oceana said in a statement.

Section 1401 of the bill, also known as the “project certainty” provision, would bar agencies from making changes to permits once they’ve been granted.

“Once issued, these approvals would be nearly impossible to revisit in the future, even if they were expedited, legally flawed, or if new science uncovers serious harm,” Oceana said in a statement.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, an environmental NGO based in American Samoa, told Mongabay by email that she welcomes economic development but not at the cost of jeopardizing American Samoa’s existing ocean-based economy. The U.S’s first-ever offshore critical mineral lease sale took place off America Samoa on Nov. 19, the same day BAAJA cleared the Senate.

“If progress requires weakening environmental protections, diminishing Indigenous voices, and asking communities with limited political power to shoulder disproportionate risks, then perhaps we need to reconsider our definition of progress,” she said.

The House of Representatives is expected to vote on the legislation next week.
